prompt: Which of these URLs is **same-origin** with `https://shop.example/home`?

options.text: `http://shop.example/home`
options.explanation: The scheme differs (`http` vs `https`). Origin includes the scheme, so this is cross-origin even though host and path match.

options.text: `https://shop.example/admin?x=1`
options.explanation: Correct. Scheme, host and (default) port 443 all match. Path and query string are not part of the origin.

options.text: `https://www.shop.example/home`
options.explanation: `www.shop.example` is a different host. Subdomains are separate origins, although they are the same *site*.

options.text: `https://shop.example:8443/home`
options.explanation: An explicit port 8443 differs from the implicit 443, so the origin differs. Port is part of the triple.

workedExample:
Write each URL as (scheme, host, port) and compare with (https, shop.example, 443):

| URL | Triple | Match? |
|---|---|---|
| A | http, shop.example, 80 | No |
| B | https, shop.example, 443 | Yes |
| C | https, www.shop.example, 443 | No |
| D | https, shop.example, 8443 | No |

Only B matches on all three. The path `/admin` and query `?x=1` are ignored.

prompt: A page on `https://evil.example` runs `fetch("https://bank.example/transfer", {method: "POST", body: "to=x"})`. The bank sends no CORS headers. What happens?

options.text: The browser refuses to send the request at all
options.explanation: This is the common misconception. A `POST` with a form-style body is a simple request, so it is sent without any preflight. The SOP blocks reading the response, not sending it.

options.text: The request is sent and processed, but the script cannot read the response
options.explanation: Correct. Simple cross-origin requests go out; without `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` the browser hides the response from the script. Any side effect on the server has already happened.

options.text: The request is sent, and the script can read the response because it was a POST
options.explanation: The method does not grant read access. Only a matching `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header does.

options.text: The server rejects it automatically because the Origin header is foreign
options.explanation: Servers do nothing with `Origin` unless their code checks it. The SOP is enforced by the browser, not the server.

workedExample:
1. Is it a simple request? Method POST: yes. A string body is sent as `text/plain`, which is safelisted. No custom headers. So no preflight.
2. The browser sends it, with an `Origin: https://evil.example` header.
3. The bank processes it. If it changes state, the change happens.
4. The response has no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, so the `fetch` promise rejects and the script sees nothing.

This gap (requests go out, reads are blocked) is exactly why CSRF defences are needed.

options.text: It lets a server tell browsers which other origins may read its responses, relaxing the same-origin policy
options.explanation: Correct. CORS is an opt-in relaxation: the server grants read access to named origins via response headers.

options.text: It protects an API from requests made by scripts on other sites
options.explanation: CORS is not a server-side firewall. Simple requests are still delivered, and non-browser clients ignore CORS entirely.

options.text: It encrypts cross-origin traffic between browser and server
options.explanation: Encryption is TLS's job. CORS is just a set of HTTP headers that control browser read access.

options.text: It stops a page from embedding cross-origin images and scripts
options.explanation: Embedding is allowed by default and CORS doesn't block it. Headers like `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy` restrict embedding, not CORS.

workedExample: Start from the SOP: by default, scripts cannot read cross-origin responses. CORS adds headers (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `-Credentials`, `-Methods`, `-Headers`) through which the *server* says "origin X may read this". So CORS can only ever add permissions. A missing or wrong CORS header makes things stricter for the browser user, but does nothing to stop `curl` hitting the endpoint.

prompt: A SPA on `https://app.example` calls `https://api.example`. Which of these requests will the browser **preflight** with `OPTIONS`? Select all that apply.

options.text: `GET /items` with only an `Accept` header
options.explanation: GET with safelisted headers is a simple request; no preflight.

options.text: `POST /items` with `Content-Type: application/json`
options.explanation: Correct. `application/json` is not one of the three safelisted content types, so it needs a preflight.

options.text: `DELETE /items/3`
options.explanation: Correct. Only GET, HEAD and POST can be simple. DELETE always triggers a preflight.

options.text: `GET /me` with an `Authorization: Bearer ...` header
options.explanation: Correct. `Authorization` is not a CORS-safelisted header, so even a GET is preflighted.

options.text: `POST /upload` with `multipart/form-data`
options.explanation: `multipart/form-data` is safelisted (an HTML form can send it), so this is a simple request.

workedExample:
Apply the three tests for a simple request:

1. Method in {GET, HEAD, POST}?
2. Only safelisted headers?
3. Content-Type in {urlencoded, multipart, text/plain}?

| Request | Fails test | Preflight |
|---|---|---|
| GET, Accept | none | No |
| POST JSON | 3 | Yes |
| DELETE | 1 | Yes |
| GET + Authorization | 2 | Yes |
| POST multipart | none | No |

The logic: anything an old HTML form could already send is simple; anything new needs permission first.

prompt:
An API responds to a credentialed `fetch` (with `credentials: "include"`) from `https://app.example` like this:

```
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
```

What does the browser do?

options.text: Lets the script read the response, since `*` matches every origin
options.explanation: The wildcard is specifically forbidden for credentialed requests. Treating `*` as "matches everything" here is the misconception.

options.text: Lets the script read the response but strips the cookies
options.explanation: The cookies were already sent with the request. The decision is about whether the script may read the response, and here it may not.

options.text: Blocks the response: with credentials, the origin must be named exactly
options.explanation: Correct. Browsers reject `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on credentialed requests, so the fetch fails with a CORS error.

options.text: Sends a second preflight asking for the exact origin
options.explanation: There's no automatic retry. The request simply fails, and the developer must fix the server's headers.

workedExample:
1. The request carries cookies because of `credentials: "include"`.
2. For credentialed responses the Fetch standard requires `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` to equal the request's origin exactly and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.
3. `*` fails the first check, so the browser treats it as a CORS failure.
4. The correct server reply is `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example` plus `Vary: Origin`, but only if that origin is on an allowlist.

prompt:
A developer checks origins like this:

```python
def allowed(origin):
    return origin.endswith(
        "example.com")
```

It reflects any allowed origin with `Allow-Credentials: true`. Which origin can an attacker register to read users' data?

options.text: `https://example.com.evil.net`
options.explanation: This ends in `evil.net`, not `example.com`, so `endswith` returns False. (A `startswith` or `in` check would fall for it.)

options.text: `https://evilexample.com`
options.explanation: Correct. The string ends with `example.com`, so the check passes, yet it is a completely separate domain anyone can register.

options.text: None: `endswith` is a safe suffix check
options.explanation: A suffix check without a leading dot accepts any domain whose name merely ends in those letters.

options.text: `null`
options.explanation: The string `"null"` does not end in `example.com`, so this check rejects it, though an allowlist that included `null` would be a separate bug.

workedExample:
Evaluate `endswith("example.com")` on each:

```
https://evilexample.com     True
https://example.com.evil.net False
null                        False
```

The fix is an exact set lookup:

```python
ALLOWED = {"https://example.com",
           "https://app.example.com"}
ok = origin in ALLOWED
```

Even `endswith(".example.com")` would trust every subdomain, including forgotten ones with XSS bugs.

prompt: Your API correctly reflects allowlisted origins in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` but omits `Vary: Origin`. A CDN caches responses. What can go wrong?

options.text: Nothing, because CORS headers are evaluated by the browser, not the CDN
options.explanation: The browser evaluates them, but the CDN decides which stored copy (with which header) to hand back. That is the problem.

options.text: The CDN may serve a response carrying origin A's header to a request from origin B, breaking B or exposing data to the wrong site
options.explanation: Correct. Without `Vary: Origin` the cache keys only on the URL, so the first origin's CORS header is reused for everyone.

options.text: Preflights stop working because OPTIONS cannot be cached
options.explanation: Preflight caching is done by the browser via `Access-Control-Max-Age`; `Vary` is about shared caches storing the main response.

options.text: The browser will refuse every response because `Vary` is mandatory in CORS
options.explanation: Browsers don't require `Vary`. It is a correctness requirement for caches, not a browser check.

workedExample:
1. Request from `https://app.example` arrives; response says `Allow-Origin: https://app.example`. CDN stores it under `/v1/config`.
2. Request from `https://admin.example` for the same URL hits the CDN. Cached copy is returned with the *app* origin in the header.
3. The admin page's fetch fails, a confusing intermittent bug.
4. Worse, if the endpoint ever reflected an untrusted origin, that permissive copy could be served widely.

`Vary: Origin` tells the cache to store a separate copy per `Origin` value.

prompt: An internal API allowlists `Origin: null` "so that local HTML files used by the support team work". Why is this dangerous?

options.text: It isn't: only `file:` pages can send `Origin: null`
options.explanation: Sandboxed iframes and some redirect chains also produce `null`, and any website can create a sandboxed iframe.

options.text: An attacker's page can embed a sandboxed iframe whose requests carry `Origin: null`, so the allowlist effectively trusts any website
options.explanation: Correct. `null` is an opaque origin that attackers can produce on demand, so trusting it is close to trusting `*` with credentials.

options.text: `null` disables the preflight, so the attacker can send DELETE requests
options.explanation: The origin value doesn't change which requests are preflighted; that depends on method and headers.

options.text: Browsers convert `null` to `*`, which breaks credentials
options.explanation: Browsers do not rewrite the value. The danger is that the allowlist matches when it shouldn't, not a conversion.

workedExample:
1. A sandboxed iframe (`sandbox` without `allow-same-origin`) gets an **opaque origin**, serialised as `null`.
2. Any site can include such an iframe and run script in it (with `allow-scripts`).
3. Its `fetch` calls send `Origin: null`.
4. The API sees `null`, finds it on the allowlist, and responds with `Allow-Origin: null` and credentials.
5. The attacker reads the victim's data.

Fix: never allowlist `null`. Serve the support tool from a real origin (e.g. `https://support.internal.example`) and allowlist that.

prompt: Which statements about cross-origin behaviour are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: A cross-origin `<script src>` runs with the including page's origin, so it can read that page's DOM
options.explanation: Correct. Script inclusion is code execution in your origin. That is why third-party scripts are a major trust decision.

options.text: Script can read the DOM of a cross-origin iframe if both pages are served over HTTPS
options.explanation: HTTPS doesn't grant access. Different host means different origin, so DOM access is blocked; the pages must use `postMessage`.

options.text: A receiver of `postMessage` should check `event.origin` before acting on the data
options.explanation: Correct. Any window can post a message to yours; checking the origin is how you know who sent it.

options.text: `https://a.example.com` and `https://b.example.com` are same-site but cross-origin
options.explanation: Correct. Hosts differ (cross-origin) but scheme and registrable domain `example.com` match (same-site).

options.text: Setting `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` restrictively prevents CSRF
options.explanation: CORS headers only control whether responses can be read. Simple requests still arrive and take effect, so CSRF needs separate defences.

workedExample:
Go through each claim using the read/write/embed split:

1. `<script src>` is embedding plus execution in *your* origin: true.
2. iframe DOM is a cross-origin *read*: blocked regardless of HTTPS.
3. `postMessage` deliberately crosses origins, so the receiver must authenticate the sender: true.
4. Origin compares full host; site compares eTLD+1: same-site, cross-origin, true.
5. CSRF is a *write*; CORS governs *reads*: false.

prompt: A team allows `https://*.example.com` (any subdomain) with credentials on their account API. A pen-tester reports a reflected XSS on the forgotten `https://old-promo.example.com`. What is the real impact?

options.text: Limited to the promo site, since XSS is confined to its own origin
options.explanation: The XSS is in the promo origin, but the API has granted that origin credentialed read access, so the impact spreads to the API.

options.text: An attacker can run script on the promo origin, call the account API with the victim's cookies and read the responses
options.explanation: Correct. The CORS allowlist turns any XSS on any trusted subdomain into a full read of the API, so the API's security is only as good as its weakest subdomain.

options.text: None, because SameSite cookies stop subdomains sending cookies
options.explanation: Subdomains of `example.com` are *same-site*, so SameSite does not block those cookies at all.

options.text: The attacker can only send requests, not read them, because of the SOP
options.explanation: The CORS headers explicitly lift the SOP for that origin, so reads are allowed.

workedExample:
1. Victim clicks a link that triggers XSS on `old-promo.example.com`.
2. The injected script runs with origin `https://old-promo.example.com`.
3. It calls `fetch("https://api.example.com/account", {credentials: "include"})`.
4. Cookies are sent (same-site, so SameSite doesn't interfere).
5. The API reflects the subdomain origin with credentials, so the browser lets the script read the account data.

Fixes: allowlist only the exact origins that need access, and decommission stale subdomains.

prompt: A preflight response includes `Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400` (24 hours). How long will Chrome cache it?

options.text: 24 hours, exactly as requested
options.explanation: Browsers cap the value. Firefox allows 24 hours, but Chromium caps it lower.

options.text: Up to 2 hours, because Chromium caps the preflight cache
options.explanation: Correct. Chromium-based browsers cap `Access-Control-Max-Age` at 7,200 seconds.

options.text: 5 seconds, because large values are ignored
options.explanation: 5 seconds is the default when the header is *absent*. A large value is clamped to the cap, not discarded.

options.text: Forever, until the user clears the cache
options.explanation: Preflight results are always time-limited; there's no permanent caching.

workedExample:
1. The header asks for 86,400 s.
2. Chromium's cap is 7,200 s (2 h); Firefox's is 86,400 s (24 h).
3. So Chrome caches for min(86,400, 7,200) = 7,200 s.
4. Without the header the default is 5 s, which is why APIs with chatty SPAs set it: otherwise many requests cost two round trips.
